title: Technical deep dive - caching + batching savings model (Suggestions beta)
topics: How Suggestions computes estimated savings for batching and caching
Telemetry required (token metering baselines, latency, throughput, cacheability signals)
Confidence intervals vs risk level and how they are shown in Console
Avoiding double-counting when batching and caching both apply
Freshness/staleness rules and when Suggestions are suppressed
summary: HelioGrid platform and SRE engineers requested a detailed explanation of how Redwood’s Suggestions beta estimates cost savings from batching and caching. They asked what telemetry is required for accurate estimates (prompt/completion tokens, request rate, latency distributions, cache hit-rate signals, and batching utilization) and how Redwood handles low-data or highly variable traffic. Redwood explained the current model: baselines derived from recent token metering windows, scenario simulation for proposed config changes (continuous batching targets, prefix/KV cache policy), and presentation of $/1M tokens plus monthly impact with a confidence interval. The team discussed why confidence is separate from risk (risk reflects potential latency/quality/SLO regression and reversibility; confidence reflects estimate stability and data quality), and confirmed guardrails for stale baselines and suppression on workloads with long-context variance. Action items include publishing a public-facing “telemetry required” table, a worked savings example, and clearer docs around estimate volatility week-to-week.
questions: What exact metrics do you need to compute caching savings, and do we have to add client-side headers?
Is the baseline based on billed tokens or raw model tokens (pre/post cache)?
How do you avoid double-counting when both caching and batching are suggested?
How do confidence intervals get computed, and what makes them widen?
If our traffic is spiky, will the estimator overfit to a lucky day?
How do you decide risk=High vs confidence=Low (or vice versa)?
Do you require request traces, or can you do it off aggregate metrics only?
action_items: Logan Wright (Redwood) - Share telemetry requirements checklist (route/model/region granularity, baseline windows, freshness thresholds) with HelioGrid - due 2026-02-14
Jonas Weber (Redwood) - Provide a worked example of $/1M token savings math for caching + batching including assumptions and confidence interval explanation - due 2026-02-18
Evan Scott (Redwood) - Send doc section clarifying billed tokens vs metered tokens vs cached tokens and where each appears in Console - due 2026-02-18
Priya Desai (HelioGrid) - Confirm current traffic split by route and whether they can enable request ID propagation for tracing hooks - due 2026-02-16
Sarah Chen (HelioGrid) - Share their current latency SLOs and p95/p99 targets per route for risk calibration discussion - due 2026-02-16
next_steps: Redwood to send a telemetry checklist + worked example docs
Schedule a 30-min follow-up to walk through HelioGrid’s top 2 routes and sanity-check estimates
HelioGrid to confirm whether they want Suggestions enabled in staging first (allowlist) before prod
transcript:
Fireflies.ai - Meeting Transcript

Title: Technical deep dive - caching + batching savings model (Suggestions beta)
Date: 2026-02-11
Time: 17:00 - 17:55 UTC
Duration: 55 minutes

Attendees (Redwood): Markus Klein, Evan Scott, Jonas Weber, Logan Wright, Hassan Mirza
Attendees (HelioGrid): Priya Desai, Miguel Alvarez, Sarah Chen, Tom Willis

---

[00:00] Markus Klein: Cool. Alright, thanks everyone for making time. This one’s intended to be like, very nerdy. We’ll go into the batching and caching economics, how the Suggestions thing is calculating numbers, and what telemetry it needs.

[00:12] Priya Desai: Perfect. Yeah, we’re basically trying to understand if the numbers are something we can trust enough to act on, even if it’s read-only in beta.

[00:22] Markus Klein: Makes sense. Evan, you wanna do the quick context on where Suggestions pulls from, and then Logan and Jonas can go deeper?

[00:28] Evan Scott: Yep. So high-level, Suggestions is taking your recent production traffic, computing a baseline cost profile per route, model, region. Then it simulates “what if we change config X”, like enabling prefix cache or increasing max batch size, and outputs delta in $/1M tokens plus an estimated monthly impact. There’s also a confidence interval based on variance and sample size.

[00:50] Tom Willis: And just to be explicit, when you say $/1M tokens, that’s… is that our billed tokens or like GPU tokens or whatever.

[00:57] Logan Wright: Good question. Right now it’s derived from metered tokens that align to what you see in Console usage—so essentially the billable token meter, but we also keep internal counters for pre-cache and post-cache. That’s part of what we show in the “basis of estimate” section.

[01:15] Miguel Alvarez: Wait, so you have both? Like tokens saved by caching would be negative tokens billed? Or is it more like we pay the same but you run cheaper.

[01:23] Hassan Mirza: It depends on deployment mode and how you price it, but conceptually caching reduces compute per request, so the effective cost per output token goes down. In the Suggestions UI we’re showing the delta in effective unit cost, not promising your invoice drops by X unless pricing is strictly token-based. That’s why it’s “estimated savings” not “guaranteed.”

[01:44] Priya Desai: That’s one of the confusion points. If we do Dedicated capacity, it’s not literally per token.

[01:49] Markus Klein: Yeah. For Dedicated we still translate to an equivalent $/1M token, because you’re basically allocating GPU time. The estimator uses your observed throughput, GPU seconds per token (derived), and then the “what if” modifies that.

[02:05] Sarah Chen: Okay, can we talk about the required telemetry? Because we’ve been burned by tools that say “insufficient data” and it’s like… we have a ton of traffic.

[02:13] Logan Wright: Totally. The minimum set is: request counts per route, prompt tokens and completion tokens, latency distributions (p50/p95), and then we need batching telemetry from the runtime—like average batch size, time in queue vs time on GPU. For caching we need cacheability signals: repeated prefixes or identical system prompts, and then actual cache hit-rate when enabled.

[02:35] Priya Desai: Do you need request payloads? Like are you hashing prompts.

[02:39] Logan Wright: No raw prompts. We don’t store prompts for this. For cacheability we compute privacy-safe fingerprints at ingest time (think hashing with tenant salt) and we aggregate counts. But for the estimator we mostly need aggregates, not per-request traces.

[02:55] Sarah Chen: Okay, so if we disable tracing, it still works.

[02:58] Logan Wright: Yeah. Tracing helps explain “why” and helps debugging, but the model runs on aggregate metrics.

[03:06] Jonas Weber: And to add: confidence is heavily affected by data quality signals. If we don’t have enough samples in the baseline window, or if the baseline is stale, we will either widen the interval or suppress a suggestion.

[03:19] Miguel Alvarez: What’s the baseline window, like last 24 hours?

[03:22] Jonas Weber: It’s configurable by estimator version, but v1 is generally last 7 days with weighting towards last 48 hours. And there’s a freshness threshold. If your metering pipeline is behind—like older than, say, 12 hours—the Suggestions view will show “telemetry delayed” and we don’t show dollar numbers.

[03:43] Tom Willis: That’s good. We’d rather see nothing than wrong numbers.

[03:46] Priya Desai: The bigger question: how are you simulating caching savings before caching is enabled. Like it sounds circular.

[03:55] Hassan Mirza: Right. So we estimate cache hit potential from prefix repetition. Example: if your system prompt plus first N tokens are identical across requests, and your user prompt has a repeated template, we can estimate a likely prefix cache hit-rate. Then we apply an expected compute reduction curve based on model and sequence length distribution.

[04:18] Priya Desai: Do you factor in that our prompts are like long-context, sometimes 30k.

[04:22] Hassan Mirza: We do, but it’s also where variance bites. Long context workloads can swing a lot. That’s where either risk gets higher or confidence goes lower, depending on what we’re seeing. Jonas maybe can explain that split.

[04:34] Jonas Weber: Yeah. So: confidence is “how stable is the estimate,” driven by sample size, variance in token lengths, and telemetry completeness. Risk is “if you implement this, what’s the chance you violate SLO or quality.” Risk uses inputs like latency headroom (your observed p95 vs target), workload variance, and reversibility. Caching can increase tail latency if your cache lookup or eviction behavior is mis-tuned, and batching can increase queueing latency.

[04:58] Sarah Chen: So you have our SLO targets?

[05:00] Markus Klein: Not automatically unless you set them in Console. In beta, we mostly infer headroom from your recent p95 and use a default threshold. But we can map to your real targets if you provide them.

[05:13] Sarah Chen: We can share p95 targets for the main routes.

[05:17] Jonas Weber: That’ll improve risk scoring.

[05:21] Miguel Alvarez: Let’s talk about batching. We already do continuous batching, but we’ve tuned it pretty conservatively. What telemetry do you need to estimate “increase max batch” savings.

[05:33] Logan Wright: We need current effective batch size distribution, queue time, and GPU utilization. If you’re at batch size 2 most of the time but could be at 6 without changing p95 too much, the simulator will project improved GPU efficiency and lower cost per token.

[05:48] Miguel Alvarez: Do you consider that higher batch might degrade output? Like if it changes RNG or something.

[05:54] Hassan Mirza: Not output quality directly for batching. It shouldn’t change outputs unless there’s nondeterminism issues, but there can be timeouts and truncation differences if latency changes. So risk is mostly latency/SLO.

[06:08] Priya Desai: Okay. Now the double counting thing. If you suggest caching AND batching, how do you avoid showing savings twice.

[06:15] Jonas Weber: Great point. The estimator computes suggestions as “atomic changes” but the savings model accounts for interaction. The baseline is your current config. Each suggestion includes an “assumptions” block saying “estimated as if applied alone.” For combined recommendations, we either (a) choose the higher-impact one first, then compute marginal savings for the second, or (b) suppress one if the marginal impact is within noise. We had a bug earlier where both were treated as independent deltas and it inflated the total. That’s fixed in current beta.

[06:47] Tom Willis: But the UI might show two numbers that we add up mentally.

[06:50] Evan Scott: Yeah, and we’re trying to be explicit: “Do not sum these.” The detail drawer will say “savings not additive.” We’re also considering a combined “plan” view later, but not in read-only beta.

[07:06] Priya Desai: Is there any chance the caching estimate is based on like a global average kernel speed, and not our deployment.

[07:13] Logan Wright: It’s based on your measured runtime stats in your region and model. We have benchmark priors, but we calibrate with your observed tokens/sec, queueing, and average seq length. If we’re missing those, confidence drops.

[07:30] Sarah Chen: What constitutes “missing”? Like do you need per-request logs?

[07:35] Logan Wright: No. But we do need route-level metrics to be correctly tagged. If everything comes in as “default route,” then we can’t separate workloads. Also if token metering is delayed, or if you’re using a gateway that strips our request IDs, some correlation features don’t work.

[07:55] Priya Desai: We do have a gateway. It’s Envoy. We might be dropping some headers.

[08:00] Evan Scott: That’s common. We can share the header allowlist you should preserve. But again, for the estimator, it’s mostly aggregates.

[08:09] Miguel Alvarez: Can you walk through an example calculation. Like a single route.

[08:15] Jonas Weber: Sure. Let’s do a simplified version. Baseline: Route “/chat/support-bot”, model “Llama-3.1-70B” (example), in us-east. We observe over 7 days: 50M total tokens, average prompt 1200, completion 300, p95 latency 1.8s, and average batch size 2.3. Effective unit cost is computed from metered cost divided by tokens, or for Dedicated, from reserved GPU hours allocated to that route (we estimate allocation using usage share).

[08:46] Tom Willis: That “allocation using usage share” is hand-wavy.

[08:49] Jonas Weber: It is a model, yes. For Dedicated the confidence interval accounts for uncertainty in attribution. For hosted it’s tighter.

[08:58] Jonas Weber: Then for batching: we simulate increasing target batch so that average batch size becomes, say, 4.0 under the observed arrival rate distribution. That reduces GPU seconds per token by X% based on the runtime curve we’ve measured. We also simulate queueing increase and check p95 headroom. Net: projected cost per 1M tokens drops by, say, $18 with an interval of [$10, $26].

[09:28] Miguel Alvarez: The arrival distribution, do you actually model time-of-day spikes.

[09:33] Logan Wright: Yes, we bucket by time and also by request rate quantiles. But if it’s super spiky—like bursts from cron jobs—variance increases and the interval widens.

[09:47] Priya Desai: That’s us. We have nightly jobs.

[09:49] Logan Wright: Then we’ll likely show “confidence: medium/low” and still provide the basis.

[09:56] Sarah Chen: What about latency. If we increase batch size, p95 might go from 1.8 to 2.4. That might violate our 2.0s target.

[10:05] Jonas Weber: Exactly. That would raise risk. Risk high doesn’t mean “don’t do it,” it means “needs validation, maybe route-specific.” The suggestion detail will list the reasons: “low latency headroom,” “high workload variance,” “limited eval coverage.”

[10:23] Priya Desai: Eval coverage—that’s the quality guardrail side?

[10:26] Jonas Weber: Yeah. For caching/batching, quality impact is usually indirect, but for some cache strategies (like aggressive prefix sharing) there are edge cases. We keep those behind guardrails and we won’t recommend them without adequate validation.

[10:43] Miguel Alvarez: Do you need us to run evals.

[10:45] Evan Scott: Not for read-only. For apply workflows later, we’ll require some checks, but that’s phase two.

[10:52] Tom Willis: I want to make sure we can explain this internally. Finance will ask: why did “estimated savings” change week to week.

[11:02] Logan Wright: Yep. Primary reasons: (1) baseline window shifts and traffic mix changes, (2) token length distribution changes, (3) metering adjustments, and (4) estimator version updates. We plan to show “last updated” and “baseline window” in UI.

[11:22] Priya Desai: Also, any unit mismatch. Like we’ve seen tokens counted differently between our client and vendor.

[11:27] Logan Wright: Yeah, tokenization differences exist. We use the model tokenizer at runtime. For comparisons, we recommend you treat our token meter as source of truth. But we can document the differences.

[11:41] Sarah Chen: Can you list the exact telemetry fields. Like names.

[11:44] Logan Wright: We can. There’s a table in the internal doc; we’ll share an externalized version. It’s basically:
- route_id, model_id, region
- prompt_tokens, completion_tokens
- request_count
- latency_ms p50/p95/p99
- queue_time_ms p50/p95
- batch_size_avg and batch_size_histogram
- cache_candidate_prefix_rate (derived)
- cache_hit_rate if enabled
- metered_cost or compute_seconds (depending on mode)

[12:20] Miguel Alvarez: “cache_candidate_prefix_rate” is new. That’s derived on your side.

[12:23] Logan Wright: Correct.

[12:26] Priya Desai: Do you require that we set route IDs. Because today we just call the same endpoint with different headers.

[12:32] Evan Scott: As long as we can segment the workload reliably. If you’re using our “route” concept with tags, that’s best. Otherwise we can infer from model + auth key, but you lose granularity.

[12:47] Sarah Chen: For Dedicated, is per-route segmentation possible.

[12:50] Markus Klein: Yes, through Console routes. And you can also segment by project/workspace.

[13:00] Miguel Alvarez: Okay. Another thing: if we enable caching, are there memory implications that might reduce batching capacity, messing up the estimate.

[13:09] Hassan Mirza: Great callout. KV/prefix cache uses GPU memory, so you might reduce max concurrency. The estimator tries to account for that by using your model memory profile and estimating headroom. That’s one area where we’re conservative; if it’s close, we label risk higher and confidence lower.

[13:31] Priya Desai: Good.

[13:33] Tom Willis: Any mention of how you treat failures. Like if cache misses spike.

[13:38] Jonas Weber: In beta, Suggestions is read-only, so there’s no runtime change. But we do track outcomes: if a customer adopts a config change (manual), we compare realized unit cost vs predicted. That helps recalibrate.

[13:55] Sarah Chen: So you track adoption. What data gets logged? We have privacy requirements.

[14:01] Evan Scott: It’s privacy-safe. Event is like “suggestion viewed/opened” and “suggestion adopted” if you tell us, with suggestion ID, route/model IDs, no prompt content.

[14:15] Priya Desai: Okay.

[14:17] Markus Klein: Maybe we can shift into Q&A on your specific routes? Or stay on model explanation.

[14:22] Priya Desai: I’d like one more thing: are confidence and risk shown separately? Because we don’t want “High risk” to always imply “Low confidence.” Sometimes you might be confident it will save money but risky for latency.

[14:35] Jonas Weber: Exactly. They’re separate. You can have: high confidence, high risk. Example: you’re very sure batching will increase efficiency, but you also know your latency headroom is thin. Or low confidence, low risk: small change with little downside, but estimate is noisy.

[14:56] Miguel Alvarez: That separation is good.

[14:58] Tom Willis: For finance, confidence is more important than risk.

[15:02] Sarah Chen: For SRE, risk is more important than confidence.

[15:04] Markus Klein: Right. That’s why we separate them.

[15:08] (crosstalk)

[15:10] Evan Scott: Also, we’re planning to explain in the detail drawer: “Risk relates to performance/quality impact; Confidence relates to estimate reliability.”

[15:24] Priya Desai: Perfect.

[15:26] Markus Klein: Ok. Let’s do route-specific quickly. Priya, you said you have two big routes. One is interactive chat, one is batch summarization.

[15:34] Priya Desai: Yep. Interactive chat needs p95 < 2 seconds. Batch can be 10 seconds, doesn’t matter. But batch is like 70% of tokens.

[15:45] Logan Wright: That’s exactly where Suggestions helps because we can propose more aggressive batching for batch route, while keeping interactive conservative.

[15:54] Miguel Alvarez: Do you provide per-route recommended batch settings.

[15:57] Hassan Mirza: We do. It’s “where it applies” in the suggestion: route/model/region.

[16:04] Sarah Chen: And it won’t suggest increasing batching for the interactive route if it’s already close to SLO.

[16:10] Jonas Weber: Correct. It might still suggest it but label risk high and the rationale will say “low latency headroom.” But we’re tuning suppression rules so we don’t spam.

[16:26] Priya Desai: Okay.

[16:28] Markus Klein: Let’s talk next steps. Logan and Jonas will send the telemetry checklist and worked example. Priya, if you can confirm header behavior in Envoy, that helps us ensure we’re not losing route tags.

[16:41] Priya Desai: Yep. I’ll check with our gateway config.

[16:45] Tom Willis: And can you add a doc section specifically: “why did the estimate change.” Like bullet list.

[16:51] Evan Scott: Yep, we’ll add that.

[16:54] Sarah Chen: Also if you can define “stale telemetry” threshold, that’s key.

[16:59] Logan Wright: We’ll include the exact thresholds and where they show up in UI.

[17:04] Markus Klein: Great. We’ll schedule a follow-up for next week to go over your top two routes and see what the Suggestions page would show. Anything else before we drop?

[17:14] Miguel Alvarez: No, this was good. Thank you.

[17:16] Priya Desai: Thanks.

[17:18] Markus Klein: Awesome. Talk soon.

---
